jabeDee — Case studyIntroduction

Product design & build

Store data in. This week’s tasks out.

jabeDee is a marketing assistant for small WooCommerce stores. It reads sales, stock and customer data, finds the money quietly leaking out of the store, and turns it into a short, ranked list of tasks, each with the tool to get it done.

jabeDee — Case studyOverview01 / 12

Dashboards say what happened. Store owners want to know what to do this week.

Small online stores have plenty of order and stock data, yet they still make their most expensive decisions by gut feeling: what to reorder, what to discount and which customers to win back. Analytics tools are built for analysts; they show charts, not the next move.

jabeDee answers one question, on the schedule the owner picks: which few tasks will protect the most sales? Everything, from the connection flow to how numbers are shown, is designed to take the owner from “I don’t know where to start” to “Done” in a few minutes.

Research method. The research is the designer’s own: desk research on stock and sales management in small stores, WooCommerce’s official documentation and a set of hypotheses about a store owner’s working week. All numbers in the screenshots are sample data.

jabeDee — Case studyProblem & users02 / 12

Three ways to lose sales, and none of them shows up on a sales chart.

01

Stock-outs

A best-seller sells out before the supplier’s order arrives. Sales stop and customers buy elsewhere. The loss is invisible because it never became a sale.

Stock, day by dayLost salesOrder arrives
02

Dead stock

Cash sits in items that haven’t sold for 90 days, money asleep on the shelf while the owner orders something else.

● 90 days without a sale
03

Lapsed customers

Someone who bought several times hasn’t come back, and nobody has reached out. A timely message could have brought the next order.

One customer’s orders60 days of silence
jabeDee — Case studyCore users02 / 12

Three people, three different weeks, one shared list.

Three personas guided the decisions. All three are based on the designer’s research and hypotheses about running a small store.

A
Persona A
The do-it-all owner

Runs a store with a few hundred products, often alone. Reorders from memory and spreadsheets, and wants a short list, not a dashboard.

B
Persona B
The buyer on a small team

Needs a defensible reason for every order quantity and a history of what was ordered before.

C
Persona C
The multi-store owner

Runs two or three stores with a teammate and wants every store’s tasks in one view.

jabeDee — Case studyStrategy03 / 12

One repeating cycle. Everything else serves it.

The product is built around a habit. On the day and hour the owner chose, a fresh list arrives. They work through it in order, each task gets a “Done” stamp, and its result is compared with before. Closing the loop is what makes the next round sharper.

  • 01Connect. Read-only, approved inside WooCommerce’s own dashboard.
  • 02Schedule. Daily, weekly, every two weeks or monthly.
  • 03Task list. Ranked by the money behind each task, with the math.
  • 04Act. Order list, SMS or discount, only with the owner’s approval.
  • 05Results. Compared with before, in the results log.

jabeDee — Case studyDesign principles03 / 12

Six principles behind every screen.

Every design decision, from layout to button copy, was tested against these six principles. When two options both looked right, the higher principle won.

01

Decision first, data second

Every screen opens with “what to do”. Charts sit next to the decision, never in its place.

02

One point of focus

Only one element per screen carries the most visual weight, so the eye lands on sales at risk first.

03

Show the math

Every number traces back to its inputs. Trust comes from being able to check the work.

04

From insight to action

Each task carries its tool: an order list, an SMS draft, a discount code or a post image.

05

Honest by default

No sales figure is ever promised, and every sample is labelled “sample”.

06

Persian-first

Right-to-left layout, Persian numerals and rounded numbers are the foundation, not a later fix.

jabeDee — Case studyConnection · the riskiest moment04 / 12

Asking a stranger for API keys is where most products lose their users.

The connection flow asks only for the store’s address. Read-only access is approved inside WooCommerce’s own dashboard and the key comes back automatically. On the same screen the owner picks a report schedule, so the product’s rhythm matches the store’s from day one.

We can
  • Read orders
  • Read products and stock
  • Read prices
We can’t
  • Change prices or stock
  • See payment details
  • Create discount codes without permission
When the host blocks it.

Some hosts and security plugins stop automatic approval. The flow explains why and offers a manual key instead.

jabeDee — Case studyDashboard · new module05 / 12

The dashboard sums up every module on one screen.

The “This week” screen says what to do; the dashboard shows where the whole store stands. Four key numbers, the sales-at-risk trend over the last six periods and one tile per module: orders, customers, kits, SMS, automation, suppliers, products, SEO and the sales calendar.

01

Sales at risk is the only dark card; the rest stay quiet so the eye lands there first.

02
Trend and result

The green bar is the share of sales at risk saved by finishing tasks.

03
Nine tiles, nine modules

Each tile has a key number and a small chart, and links to its module.

04
Aware of plan and schedule

Locked modules are blurred, and labels follow the report schedule.

jabeDee — Case studyThe core05 / 12

Tick a task and the stamp lands.

Each row is one decision. Once it’s done, the row steps back, a stamp marks it and the progress bar moves, so the list always shows what’s left. The stamp is the panel’s only playful moment, saved for finished work.

jabeDee — Case studyFrom insight to action06 / 12

Most tools stop exactly where the work begins.

In jabeDee every suggestion is wired to the tool that carries it out. The owner never leaves the app to act on a task, and no message is sent without their final approval.

01

Ready-made kits. For every sales opportunity, a kit with audience, copy and steps; each kit’s result is measured afterwards.

02

A discount kit. Two offers, a discount code and four steps that are ticked off one by one.

03

Send an SMS. Four steps: audience, message, timing and review. The audience is read live and never stored.

04

Instagram studio. A post or story image built from the same kit and downloaded.

jabeDee — Case studyNew feature · report schedule07 / 12

Every store has its own rhythm, so the schedule is the owner’s call.

The previous version had a single weekend report. But a busy store needs a fresh list every day, and a seasonal one maybe once a month. Now the owner chooses daily, weekly, every two weeks or monthly, plus the day and hour.

It isn’t just a setting. The whole panel adapts: the home headline, the report’s name, the date range and even the window used to measure each kit’s results.

jabeDee — Case studyTrust & decisions08 / 12

Trust is built into the product, not into the marketing copy.

DecisionWhy
01Access

Read-only; discount codes need separate permission.

Owners won’t hand their store to a tool they don’t know yet. Asking for less reduces drop-off at connection.

02Customer data

Names and numbers are never stored; lists are read live from the store.

Less security burden and a simple answer to every owner’s first question.

03Automation

Rules only create drafts, and every draft waits in an approval inbox.

A wrong SMS to hundreds of customers can’t be undone; the last call stays human.

04Alerts

Simple, explainable rules instead of a learning model.

A rule can be shown on screen. A model would weaken “show the math”.

05Results

Before-and-after reporting, no numeric promises.

A product that promises to double sales loses trust on its first bad week.

Automation approval inbox. Every draft waits for the owner to approve or reject it.

jabeDee — Case studyBrand · redesign09 / 12

From JabehD to jabeDee: a brand that feels like someone’s desk.

The previous version was a tidy, neutral dashboard in navy, cream and teal. It worked, but it looked like dozens of other tools. In the redesign the brand grew out of the owner’s own question: big Persian headlines, a yellow marker for the one number that matters, tasks as notes on a desk and a “Done” stamp for finished work. The panel stays deliberately calm; the brand lives in the details.

jabedee.ir

The marketing site. The owner’s question is the headline and the notes show the product itself.

Name

From “JabehD” to “jabeDee”: shorter, more memorable, same “data box” root.

Colour

Deep teal for trust; marker yellow only for the most important number on a screen.

Typography

Lalezar for brand headlines, Vazirmatn for interface and numbers.

Motifs

Sticky notes, a “Done” stamp and a torn paper edge, all from the world of a desk.

Voice

Everyday language, no marketing jargon; every promise on the site is something the product actually does.

One file, works offline.

The whole app is built with modular TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4 and esbuild into a single HTML file of about 660 KB. Navigation happens inside the app, so every button works even in sandboxed previews, and Playwright tests every screen on desktop and mobile.

jabeDee — Case studyReflection

The best interface decision in this project was removing questions: no API key, no bank card and never asking which chart to look at.
